text.content: Vela Systems has been running its multi-agent internal tooling for a few weeks. In a single-session test with one agent and one user, everything worked. The memory boundary decisions held. The state handoffs completed cleanly. State recovered correctly when the session was interrupted. But now the Vela team is planning to open the system to their full customer operations group, thirty users across two teams, running queries simultaneously across the three specialist agents. And the question on the table is not "does it work?" They've already established that. The question is: "does it still work at scale, and will we know when it doesn't?"

text.content: This lesson addresses both halves of that question. The first half is about how memory and state behave differently when the system is under load from multiple concurrent users. The second half is about observability, specifically, what to log so that when something goes wrong across a multi-agent system, you can trace the failure rather than guess at it.

text.content: How scale changes the memory picture

rich_text.plain_text: How scale changes the memory picture

text.content: When one user runs one query, memory boundaries feel clean and self-evident. The context window belongs to the session. Flow State keys update in a clear sequence. Nothing competes for write access.

rich_text.plain_text: When one user runs one query, memory boundaries feel clean and self-evident. The context window belongs to the session. Flow State keys update in a clear sequence. Nothing competes for write access.

text.content: When thirty users run queries concurrently, some hitting the Classifier, some mid-handoff to a specialist, some waiting on a second-agent reply, the picture gets more complicated in two specific ways.

rich_text.plain_text: When thirty users run queries concurrently, some hitting the Classifier, some mid-handoff to a specialist, some waiting on a second-agent reply, the picture gets more complicated in two specific ways.

text.content: Context windows scale cleanly. Flow State does not.

rich_text.plain_text: Context windows scale cleanly. Flow State does not.

text.content: Each user session gets its own context window. There is no sharing, no competition, no cross-contamination. The architecture already isolates sessions by design, so concurrency at the context-window level is not a problem.

rich_text.plain_text: Each user session gets its own context window. There is no sharing, no competition, no cross-contamination. The architecture already isolates sessions by design, so concurrency at the context-window level is not a problem.

text.content: Flow State is different. If your agents write to a shared Flow State key (a key that is not scoped per session), then thirty concurrent sessions are writing to the same location. The last write wins. Earlier writes are silently overwritten. This is not a bug you will see in testing; it only surfaces when two sessions are mid-execution at the same moment.

text.content: Persistent store reads accumulate.

rich_text.plain_text: Persistent store reads accumulate.

text.content: In a single-session system, a lookup to a persistent store (a Qdrant collection, an Airtable base, an external API) is one call per query. In a thirty-user concurrent system, those calls multiply. The total lookup volume is determined by how many agents perform reads and how many sessions are running simultaneously.

text.content: Systems that performed one persistent-store call per query in testing may perform thirty in production during peak load. This is a reason to be deliberate about which agent performs them, and whether a result can be carried forward in Flow State rather than re-fetched by each agent in the chain.

text.content: In a single-agent system, tracing a failure is relatively simple: the agent either completed or it did not, and the output is the evidence. In a multi-agent system, a failure can occur at any of several decision points: at the Classifier, in the handoff contract between agents, in a specialist's state write, or in the recovery logic after an interruption. Log nothing, and all you know is that the output was wrong. Log the right things, and you can read backward from the output to the specific agent and decision that produced it.

text.content: Summary

rich_text.plain_text: Summary

text.content: A multi-agent system that works in testing can fail in production under concurrent load, and the failures are difficult to diagnose without the right log entries. Context windows scale cleanly because they are session-isolated by design. Flow State does not scale cleanly if any key is written globally rather than per session. This is a production consequence of the memory boundary decisions from Sprint 3, not a new problem.

text.content: Observability across a multi-agent system requires logging at four positions: query classification, state written before handoff, state read on specialist entry, and reply written. Together these four positions form a trace that spans the entire execution chain. Any gap in the trace identifies the specific agent and handoff where a failure occurred.
